title: Verdigris Systems - Key Handover & Egress Guardrails Review
summary: Deep dive on private deployment security posture: network isolation, egress controls, KMS key handoff, SSO integration and audit logging. Agreed next steps include sharing SOC2 artifacts, a control-plane diagram, and scheduling a short bench test for egress throughput.
topics: Customer-managed KMS key provisioning and rotation
Audit log retention and SIEM integration
action_items: Maya Chen - Share SOC 2 Type II summary + controls matrix - 2026-09-08
Liam Ortiz - Produce per-subnet egress diagram with proposed NAT/proxy and ports - 2026-09-07
Elena Sokolova - Provide current onprem firewall rules and upstream proxy config (sample) - 2026-09-06
next_steps: Redwood to email security pack and control-plane diagram
Schedule 30-min bench to exercise egress proxy and measure latency/throughput
Customer to confirm KMS provider and whether HSM-backed keys required
transcript:
Header: 2026-09-03 14:00 PDT | Duration: 62m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Ravi (Verdigris Head of Security), Elena (Infra), Daniel (CTO), Priya (Legal)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for carving out the time, we thought we'd run through the private deployment checklist, focus on the KMS handoff and egress guardrails
[00:22] Ravi: yep thanks, quick context — Verdigris is doing regulated telemetry processing, so data residency + no external exfil is a hard req. We're evaluating Redwood Private for model serving inside our co-lo.
[00:37] Liam: great, can I ask what your current network layout looks like, like are you running a single L3 VRF or multiple isolated racks?
[00:45] Elena: currently two racks, separate VLANs per environment. We use a customer-provided gateway that terminates TLS and funnels outbound through an upstream proxy that does allowlisting.
[01:02] Liam: ok so the natural fit is Redwood Private with a control plane that can be air-gapped or a customer-managed control-plane endpoint; for egress we recommend an explicit egress proxy pattern — the inference nodes only talk to the proxy on allowed ports.
[01:23] Daniel: question: when you say "control plane" can the control plane also be hosted by Redwood but reachable only via private link? we need to know the telemetry we send is minimal and encrypted.
[01:36] Maya: yes options: hosted control plane over PrivateLink or a customer-managed control plane. For SOC2 customers we typically provide a VPC endpoint with mutual TLS, minimal telemetry, and opt-in debug logs.
[01:52] Ravi: and audit log retention? we need to keep a 7-year trail for certain flows, and logs must ship to our SIEM (Splunk).
[02:04] Liam: Redwood can export audit events to customer Kinesis/HTTP sink or push to S3 with KMS envelope encryption. Retention is policy-driven; we'll surface event IDs for model payloads, inference request context, and auth events.
[02:22] Priya: legal question: any PII in logs by default? we need guarantees around scrubbing and redaction.
[02:31] Maya: by default we do not log full prompt contents in high-retention audit; prompts are configurable. For regulated work we'd recommend redaction at ingestion and token-level masks. We can include this in the controls matrix.
[02:48] Elena: about keys — we want to manage keys in-house using our HSM. can Redwood run using customer-managed KMS keys or must the platform own the root?
[03:01] Liam: yes you can bring your own keys. Two modes: 1) bring-your-own-KMS where Redwood obtains short-lived DEKs via customer KMS (recommended), or 2) islanded mode where keys never leave your HSM and encryption/decryption happens in your network. Both have tradeoffs for ops complexity.
[03:23] Ravi: islanded mode sounds safer but means we need to host enclaves for model serving?
[03:30] Liam: not enclaves necessarily — we support running the runtime in your network with KMS calls to your HSM. For highly sensitive workloads you can disable persistent debug and require HSM attestations on rollout.
[03:47] Daniel: latency implications for KMS calls? will every token require a KMS roundtrip?
[03:53] Liam: no — we use DEKs for per-instance encryption and only use KMS for key wrapping/unwrapping at boot or rotation. So steady-state inference isn't hitting KMS per request.
[04:07] Maya: let's pivot to egress: typical pattern is an egress proxy (squid/varnish/istio-egress) that does TLS origination to allowed destinations. Redwood supports a static allowlist of domains and IPs and also supports per-customer egress via NAT gateway.
[04:25] Elena: we enforce deep packet inspection on our upstream proxy, we'd want the Redwood nodes to use mTLS to the proxy so DPI doesn't see plaintext.
[04:33] Liam: yes mTLS to proxy is supported. We'll provide CA bundles and the nodes will authenticate with certs we provision or you can provision certs via your PKI.
[04:45] Ravi: what about fallback behavior? if the egress proxy fails, do nodes go direct to internet? that's unacceptable.
[04:52] Liam: we have strict network policies: no direct internet egress unless a route is explicitly configured. If proxy is unreachable nodes will fail requests per policy; we can optionally queue locally for a short time but not exfiltrate.
[05:06] Priya: we also need an attestation trail for rollouts — who triggered a new model, and what code hash. does Redwood provide provenance?
[05:15] Maya: yes we include rollout audit events with user identity, commit hash, deploy artifact ID, and can include automation tokens. Those are shipped to your audit sink.
questions: Can Redwood use our on-prem HSM for key wrapping?
What events are included in long-term audit exports?
How does fallback work if egress proxy fails?
